papers.title: Robust Posterior Projection for Bayesian Inference Under Order Restrictions
papers.abstract: In archaeology and geochronology, stratigraphic information constrains the relative chronological order of dated samples. Bayesian chronological models incorporate these constraints either through the prior, or by projecting an unconstrained posterior distribution onto the set of ordered chronologies. Dating measurements may nevertheless appear inconsistent with their stratigraphic position, owing to disturbances that do not justify discarding them. We introduce different robust projection maps based on the Huber loss and characterize the non-uniqueness of the considered maps which justifies a Tikhonov regularization. The robust maps also decompose each sample into a monotone baseline and a spike, which flags questionable samples. We adapt the Sequential Block Merging algorithm for the Huber-type losses, and propose a data-driven heuristic for selecting the hyperparameter on which each loss depends on. Simulation studies and geochronological case studies illustrate the gains in robustness and their limits.

papers.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
papers.abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.

papers.title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform
papers.abstract: The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber--Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.

papers.title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics
papers.abstract: This study focuses on regression estimation and variable selection based on target data, while incorporating information from coefficient estimates obtained in related studies. A weighted combination of these estimates may agree with some target effects but differ from others. We propose Transfer Regression with Adaptive Credibility Estimation (TRACE), a Bayesian method requiring only fitted coefficients and sample sizes from source studies. TRACE learns simplex-constrained source weights shared across variables. Separate latent indicators determine target inclusion and whether each coefficient is guided by the weighted source estimate. We develop an approximate collapsed variational expectation-maximization algorithm with robust source-weight initialization. Under suitable conditions, consistency of variable selection, transfer decisions, and source-weight estimation is established. These results hold at every prespecified fixed iteration in fixed dimension and at global mean-field optima of the exact collapsed variational objective as the dimension grows. Simulations show that TRACE achieves competitive variable-selection performance under different patterns of source heterogeneity. An application to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project illustrates its use in cross-tissue gene-expression prediction.

papers.title: The Fragility Of Synthetic Populations Over Time: An Evaluation Of Forecasting Strategies For Agent-Based Models
papers.abstract: Agent-based simulation models are widely used to assess the future mobility projects. However, their effectiveness hinges on the accuracy of synthetic populations, which are often generated using data from a single reference year. This study explores the temporal validity of these populations by evaluating their performance over multi-year datasets in a simulation-like environment. We focus on multi-dimensional agents, ensuring that all attributes critical to the simulation are comprehensively represented. To assess the quality of synthetic populations, we compare three generation methods: direct use of original training data, Bayesian Network sampling, and diffusion model. We then evaluate four agent-forecasting approaches: static projection (both idealistic and realistic), resampling, and dynamic projection. While dynamic projection holds potential, it requires complex longitudinal data to model the evolution of agent attributes. To address this, we introduce a heuristic model based on aggregated statistics, though its limitation lies in ignoring attribute correlations, which reduces its accuracy. Our results demonstrate that synthetic populations lose relevance over time, emphasizing the necessity of effective agent-forecasting. Among the methods tested, idealistic static projection yields the best performance but requires data that is difficult to obtain. The other methods show limited improvements, highlighting the ongoing challenges in accurately forecasting agent attributes.

papers.title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations
papers.abstract: Iterative algorithms are integral to many statistical procedures, whereas sampling uncertainty along their iteration is generally not quantified. We develop simultaneous inference for discrete trajectories generated from high-dimensional estimating equations, with iteration-specific population estimands that preserve algorithmic regularization. Our proposed fixed-Jacobian bootstrap propagates perturbations along the observed trajectory without repeatedly running the original nonlinear algorithm. We establish uniform first-order expansions and bootstrap validity over possibly infinite sets of contrasts and iterations under stability, entropy and moment conditions. Simulations in sparse linear regression, paired Fisher discrimination, and temporal-difference learning demonstrate accurate simultaneous coverage. A micro-randomized trial application illustrates inference for a treatment trajectory with participant-level clustering.

papers.title: Data-Adaptive Subset-Size Selection for Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimation
papers.abstract: Subset size determines the balance between robustness and efficiency in minimum covariance determinant estimation. Conventional choices fix this balance before the extent and structure of contamination are known. Reweighting does not remove the influence of the initial subset size. We propose a data-adaptive rule based on ordered squared Mahalanobis distances. It selects the first window maximum, with window width proportional to the sample size. For a minimum covariance determinant subset, the statistic equals the smallest squared distance among excluded observations. For smooth elliptical distributions with small one-point contamination, we characterize the first population window maximum. Under suitable conditions, it is the last retained fraction at which excluding the contaminating point remains optimal. We derive a first-order expansion for this boundary and establish sample localization along the full integer path. Without contamination, the selected fraction tends to one. A fast depth-based implementation reuses one ordering across candidate sizes. Simulations under Gaussian and heavy-tailed sampling show gains over fixed subset sizes, most consistently for scatter estimation. Real data analyses show that the initial subset size affects which observations are retained after reweighting.

papers.title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption
papers.abstract: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.

papers.title: stMIND: Learning multiscale interaction dynamics from spatial-temporal transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Interactions within local cellular neighborhoods and across broader tissue scales jointly govern molecular state transitions and morphogenesis during development and regeneration. While time-resolved spatial transcriptomics simultaneously profiles gene expression and spatial coordinates, destructive sequencing samples distinct cells at each time point, leaving intermediate trajectories and multiscale intercellular interactions unobserved. Building upon our interacting mean-field neural stochastic differential equation framework, we present stMIND (Spatiotemporal Multiscale Interaction Neural Dynamics), a continuous-time generative framework that infers coupled molecular, spatial, and proliferation dynamics from unmatched spatiotemporal snapshots. stMIND decomposes cellular expression velocity vector/drift into three interpretable operators: a cell-intrinsic program, a local graph-difference attention operator that aggregates relative expression differences and spatial geometry within a co-evolving physical radius, and a nonlocal mean-field attention operator that captures long-range population context beyond the immediate neighborhood. By evolving dynamic spatial neighborhoods alongside cellular migration and enforcing orthogonality between intrinsic and interaction-driven drifts, stMIND resolves scale-specific intercellular influences through optimal transport in joint expression-position space. In axolotl and zebrafish benchmarks, stMIND leads in expression prediction, anatomical consistency and spatial coherence. Ablations confirm the need to combine disjoint local and nonlocal operators. It reveals a regenerative transition in axolotl telencephalon 10 to 15 days after injury, with a drift energy surge followed by nonlocal dominance and local counterbalance varying by cell type in reactive ependymoglial niches. It tracks developmental vector fields across zebrafish stages.

papers.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
papers.abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.

papers.title: Zero-inflated generalized linear latent variable models for microbiome compositional data
papers.abstract: In this paper, we incorporate the Dirichlet--multinomial distribution into the generalized linear latent variable model (GLLVM) framework to accommodate high-dimensional, overdispersed compositional count data and capture complex covariation among taxa with a low-rank structure. Advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have generated large amounts of microbiome count data, stimulating research into their associations with human diseases and traits. Such data are compositional and often highly sparse for various reasons, posing challenges for statistical analysis. Conventional zero-replacement approaches ignore the underlying causes of zeros, further complicating the analysis. We therefore propose a zero-inflated Dirichlet--multinomial latent variable model (ZIDM-LVM). Since the marginal likelihood has no closed-form expression, we develop a variational approximation (VA) approach for efficient parameter estimation. Simulation studies and applications to two microbiome datasets are presented to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.

papers.title: BioMARS 2.0: a robotic biologist for formulating and adapting biological experiments
papers.abstract: Biological experimentation is not reducible to a single optimization problem, but requires decisions at multiple levels of abstraction: translating scientific knowledge into experimental procedures, adapting culture conditions to measured phenotypes and selecting interventions that test biological hypotheses. Automating experimental execution does not, by itself, determine which experiments should be performed next or how they should change in response to biological feedback. Here we introduce BioMARS, a human-in-the-loop multi-agent robotic system that connects knowledge-guided experimental decision-making with robotic execution and biological feedback. At the procedural level, BioMARS generated literature-grounded protocols and traceable action plans, improving expert-reviewed protocol quality scores across four model backends. At the parametric level, BioMARS used image-derived phenotypes from robotic retinal organoid culture to select subsequent experimental conditions, with higher reported scores in later rounds of the three-round experiment. At the intervention level, BioMARS nominated drug-repurposing candidates from biomedical evidence and advanced six candidates to wet-lab testing by researchers. Together, these studies demonstrate feedback-driven robotic biological experimentation within a framework that supports decisions about experimental procedures, culture conditions and biological interventions.

papers.title: Short-term associations between wild-bird and mammalian high pathogenic avian influenza detection in the United States
papers.abstract: High pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) detections in mammals have raised concern about repeated wildlife spillover and the targeting of mammalian surveillance. We evaluated whether wild-bird detection records contained short-term explanatory and predictive information about mammalian detections in the United States. Public surveillance records from April 2022 to July 2026 comprised 18,523 wild-bird and 815 mammalian detections. Monthly state-level mammalian counts were analysed using negative-binomial mixed models adjusted for seasonality, preceding mammalian detections and state-level heterogeneity. The selected model contained contemporaneous and one-month-lagged same-state wild-bird counts. A doubling of one plus the contemporaneous wild-bird count was associated with a 57.9% increase in the expected mammalian count (95% CI 43.5-73.8%), and a doubling of the preceding-month count with a 15.9% increase (5.2-27.8%). Bordering-state exposure did not improve fit. In a six-month temporal holdout, adding same-state wild-bird exposure reduced mean absolute error by 23.8% and root mean squared error by 27.9%, although total detections remained overpredicted. After exact-row deduplication, the corresponding effects were 59.7% and 13.3%. Wild-bird surveillance records contained short-term, geographically local information about mammalian HPAI detection activity, but the associations do not establish direct transmission and require further calibration before operational forecasting.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.

papers.title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data
papers.abstract: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.

papers.title: Characterizing Underrepresentation when Generalizing Causal Survival Estimates
papers.abstract: Randomized trial findings are routinely generalized to broader target populations to inform decisions in medicine and public policy. When the trial sample is misaligned with the target population, generalized effect estimates can yield suboptimal decisions. We characterize the target subgroups that are underrepresented in the trial cohort in time-to-event settings. Here, underrepresentation arises in two distinct ways: baseline underrepresentation, when a subgroup's covariate profile is rare in the trial relative to the target, and time-varying underrepresentation, when differential censoring erodes a subgroup over follow-up. Existing diagnostics either conflate these mechanisms or apply only to the baseline case. We show that the asymptotic variance of the efficient generalizability estimator admits a decomposition in which only two terms can diverge as representation weakens: a sampling-weight term capturing baseline misalignment and a censoring-weight term capturing differential loss to follow-up. Underrepresented subgroups are therefore those with imprecise generalized estimates, and the larger of the two terms gives the responsible channel. We use this decomposition in TRACE (Temporal Rashomon Analysis of CEnsored data), which combines a self-normalized variance objective with a tree-based search to localize underrepresented subgroups, attribute each to baseline mismatch or censoring, and find the follow-up intervals where censoring drives the variance inflation. We solve the joint problem with a parametric dynamic program nested inside a Rashomon ensemble of near-optimal trees. In synthetic benchmarks, TRACE recovers the planted underrepresented regions. In a case study generalizing the National Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) Study to U.S. JTPA-eligible adults, restricting to reliably generalizable subgroups narrows the 95% confidence interval for the refined estimand by 60%.

papers.title: Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding
papers.abstract: Causal mediation analysis of cluster-randomized trials can reveal how interventions affect outcomes through individual and spillover pathways. Most existing methods target natural mediation effects under assumptions that exclude treatment-induced mediator--outcome confounding. We develop a semiparametric framework for interventional mediation effects that accommodates such confounding and within-cluster interference without requiring cross-world independence assumptions. We identify cluster-average and individual-average direct and indirect effects and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components, distinguishing pathways through an individual's own mediator and those of other cluster members. These contrasts evaluate hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways represented by natural effects, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective that complements natural effects. We derive efficient influence functions to construct estimators using cluster-level cross-fitting, characterize their multiple-robustness properties, and establish conditions for asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency. To facilitate implementation, we develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization that reduces the need for multivariate density estimation and integration and allows nuisance functions to be estimated using parametric models or machine learning. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample performance, and an application to a cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain illustrates the proposed methods.

papers.title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes
papers.abstract: Log-optimal e-variables at fixed horizons, also called numéraires, have been conjectured to ``almost'' form an e-process for exponential-family null hypotheses. A related open question is whether an e-process can attain the optimal e-power at every horizon up to a bounded loss. Given a final horizon, we study the minimax regret of e-processes relative to the numéraires at all times up to it. For the Gaussian location null and the composite alternative of Gaussian distributions with a smaller variance and an unknown location, we show that the minimax regret in the worst case over the location grows like the iterated logarithm of the final horizon. A single e-process attains this rate at every horizon. This growth answers the question negatively. It also refutes the conjecture if ``almost'' means a regret bounded uniformly over horizons. For this Gaussian location problem, we thus exhibit the frontier precisely: the minimax regret is bounded if and only if the alternatives have at least the variance of the null.

papers.title: Distribution-Free Symmetry Detection in Multi-Reference Alignment at Low SNR
papers.abstract: Symmetry can reveal the structure of a signal, but detecting it becomes difficult when observations are noisy and randomly transformed. We study how to infer symmetry directly from multi-reference alignment data with additive isotropic Gaussian noise of known variance, without aligning the observations or knowing how the transformations were sampled. For cyclic symmetry, we identify a simple statistical signature that yields tests with exact finite-sample error guarantees. We demonstrate their performance even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. Dihedral symmetry presents a deeper challenge: we show that, for some signals, invariant moments below a sharp order threshold cannot distinguish reflectional from purely rotational symmetry. For generic signals, however, this distinction emerges much earlier. We use these insights to develop tests for dihedral symmetry with asymptotic error control under explicit nondegeneracy conditions. Together, the results clarify what we can learn about symmetry from noisy, unaligned data and suggest a path toward symmetry inference in cryo-EM.

papers.title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.

papers.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

papers.title: On the robustness of locally D-optimal designs under parameter uncertainty in single-factor generalized linear models
papers.abstract: Local and Bayesian approaches to optimal experimental design specify information about the regression parameters through a nominal value and a prior distribution, respectively. A practical question is whether accounting for parameter uncertainty justifies replacing a locally optimal design. We investigate when locally D-optimal designs remain Bayesian D-optimal in single-factor Poisson, gamma and logistic regression on the unit interval. Analytical arguments and numerical comparisons under normal and uniform slope priors examine how prior form and dispersion affect the optimal support and the Bayesian D-efficiency of retaining a local design.

papers.title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection
papers.abstract: Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. Heavy-tailed returns and dependence across funds complicate this task. We propose a robust selection procedure based on radially weighted alpha estimation in linear factor pricing models. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. For radial weights fixed conditional on the factor design, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control under elliptically symmetric errors and show that the proportion of sufficiently strong positive-alpha funds selected tends to one. The theory accommodates comparable cross-sectional and time-series dimensions and nonvanishing alphas. We also develop a smoothed implementation and assess its finite-sample properties. Simulations show higher true discovery proportions than least-squares and spatial-sign methods under heavy-tailed distributions and improved numerical stability from smoothing. An application to U.S. equity mutual funds examines the subsequent performance of portfolios formed from the selected funds.

papers.title: Reproducible quantum clustering for single-cell transcriptome atlases
papers.abstract: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and can yield inconsistent clusters across random seeds. We introduce KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework for reproducible whole-transcriptome clustering. KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, enabling exact feature evaluation on classical hardware and direct checks on a quantum processor. Theoretically, we prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally. Practically, while retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, KQE-2 delivered identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes, the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79. KQE-2 scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, outperforming the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases (and within the best method's run-to-run range on two), and leads on six even under standard downstream clustering.

papers.title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Measurement systems generate uncertain information that downstream manufacturing decisions often consume as if fixed. This structured integrative review examines how measurement error, uncertainty, GR\&R estimates, calibration evidence, and drift information are handed off into capability inference, retrospective Phase I reference estimation, prospective Phase II monitoring, operational action, and requalification. Studies are compared by the upstream uncertain object, whether it is known, calibrated, or estimated, its propagation mechanism, the downstream decision, and the validation boundary. The synthesis distinguishes recorded production data from latent-process targets: measurement-system information calibrates limits, uncertainty statements, replication, guard bands, or losses, but does not reveal the realized random error in an individual record. Within the retained literature, measurement-to-capability and measurement-to-monitoring mechanisms are more extensively represented by model-based studies, whereas prospective evidence is thinner where statistical results must support source attribution, cost-sensitive action, and requalification. A decision-handoff spine separates measurement generation, statistical inference, and operational validation so that capability, stability, attribution, and intervention effectiveness are not conflated. The review is integrative rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is an auditable measurement-science framework that preserves provenance, information status, validity conditions, and downstream use while identifying claims that are model-supported, conditionally calibrated, or not yet operationally validated.

papers.title: Can the Remaining Answers Change the Prediction? Worst-Case Stability Checks for Personalized Rating Models
papers.abstract: Missing ratings can overturn a personalized model's current prediction. For completed models with additive response scores, exact worst case bounds check all missing assignments without changing the current predictor. We evaluate this audit retrospectively in two self-triage cohorts, 108 clinicians rating three simulated psychiatric interviews, and 126 counseling demonstrations annotated by ten experts. Under shared random half histories, Fisher adaptation based on observed ratings reduces log loss relative to response frequency by 0.1071 nats in the clinician audit (95% CI [0.0867,0.1261]) and 0.0223 in counseling (95% CI[0.0121,0.0321]). The counseling test excludes target experts and source videos from training. Certification covers 5.4% and 10.5% of targets; fixed width acquisition raises coverage to 13.7% and 28.6% at the same budgets. With weights and responses held fixed, the observed-rating update also has lower loss than an affine partial update while certifying exactly the same evaluated targets. The certificate establishes agreement with the completed model, not correctness or stability at intermediate updates. These rating tasks test the method; clinical usefulness remains untested.

papers.title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records
papers.abstract: Representations learned from electronic health record (EHR) data encode patient physiology together with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when, and for whom. We formalize the data-generating process with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation, and clinical environments, and analyze two strategies for undoing this entanglement. First, no division of the information carried by laboratory "value" and "ordering" channels is identified from a single dataset: when ordering depends on the analyte, its distribution among untested patients is not recoverable, and a sentinel code for the undefined recorded value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator, fixing partial information decomposition (PID) for every redundancy measure satisfying the Williams-Beer axioms and invariant under injective re-encoding. Second, cross-site invariance of representation-conditional outcomes is a falsifiable implication of biological invariance taken jointly with exclusion and representation-sufficiency conditions, but not an identification strategy: we construct observationally equivalent models that disagree about biological invariance, whether the invariance test fails or passes. For binary physiology this happens exactly when case mix differs, the representation is lossy, and physiology affects the outcome. A worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism. Tests performed for every patient remove the ordering gate, and measured tests can restore identification: biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology, or, for binary physiology, when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix. Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis.

papers.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups
papers.abstract: We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. Maximum-statistic procedures exploit the correlation between subgroups' statistics, but calibration decides what they protect. Re-randomization controls error exactly when treatment has no effect, but not when only an average effect is zero, whereas a multiplier bootstrap protects average effects only asymptotically. Our first result characterizes when re-randomization alone protects average effects. It reverses the arms' weights in the statistics' covariance, so with unequal allocation and heterogeneous effects it can overstate their correlations; in one such family of 50 subgroups, its limiting familywise error is 0.064 at nominal 0.025. We propose a step-down procedure called ATHOS, short for agreement-based testing of hypotheses in overlapping subgroups, which confirms a subgroup only when both calibrations reject it. Given assignments exchangeable within strata, ATHOS controls familywise error exactly when treatment has no effect and, under complete randomization, asymptotically for average effects, even in large families. Our second result shows that requiring agreement costs no first-order local power in balanced trials. In a null simulation with 200 patients and 1,497 subgroups, the bootstrap step-down alone made false claims in 40% of trials and ATHOS in 2.6%. In two comparisons in an HIV trial, ATHOS confirmed 188 and 73 subgroups and Holm's procedure 179 and 62.

papers.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
papers.abstract: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

papers.title: Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations
papers.abstract: Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. Without a pre-treatment trajectory to match, choosing donor weights for such post-only locations requires an additional source of information. We propose Graph-SCM, which estimates donor weights jointly across treated locations and encourages geographically neighboring locations to use similar donor combinations. GeoEco-SCM keeps the same geographic graph but adjusts the strength of its existing edges using pre-treatment economic similarity. Both methods handle complete, partial, and absent histories within one convex weight-estimation problem. Monte Carlo experiments compare them with covariate-balanced synthetic controls, equally weighted donor averages, ordinary synthetic control where estimable, and nonseparable spatio-temporal imputation and direct prediction. No method dominates. Graph-based borrowing improves on covariate balancing in several settings, but a selective-coverage design favors covariate balancing. Economic adjustment helps when geography alone misses relevant donor relationships. The results support graph regularization as a way to extend synthetic-control coverage when connected locations share similar donor representations, with its usefulness depending on the structure of the available information.

papers.title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions
papers.abstract: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.

papers.title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.

papers.title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
papers.abstract: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

papers.title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring
papers.abstract: We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.

papers.title: ZIO: Order-Based Structure Learning for Zero-Inflated Count Data under Data Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We propose a structure learning method for directed acyclic graph (DAG) models of zero-inflated multivariate count data. Although causal structure learning with zero-inflated Poisson models is identifiable, existing algorithms rely on local search over the DAG space, leading to poor scalability and a tendency to converge to suboptimal solutions. To address these limitations, we develop a novel order-based scoring framework that searches over variable orderings rather than directly over DAGs. Building on this framework, we further extend the method to multiple heterogeneous datasets by identifying a shared variable ordering while allowing each dataset to have its own edge set. We implement a stochastic hill climbing algorithm with a random-to-random (R2R) proposal operator to efficiently explore the ordering space. Simulation studies show competitive performance against existing methods and improved graph estimation accuracy as more heterogeneous datasets are jointly analyzed under a shared causal ordering. We apply the method to single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from a major depressive disorder study.

papers.title: Uniform inference for $U$-statistics of exchangeable arrays under degeneracy
papers.abstract: Many $U$-statistics of row-column exchangeable arrays become degenerate at natural null hypotheses: their convergence rates change and their limiting laws may or may not remain Gaussian. We establish conditions under which inference based on the classical unbiased variance estimator is uniformly valid across these changes, without knowledge of the degeneracy order. It is known that $U$-statistics can be decomposed into orthogonal projections indexed by bipartite graphs. Under uniform fourth-moment assumptions, we establish that the standardized statistic is asymptotically Gaussian and the classical unbiased variance estimator is ratio-consistent, as long as a certain measure of concentration for projections indexed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. Under compactness of the normalized projections, both properties hold if and only if the proportion of variance contributed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. The necessity of this condition follows from a general limit theorem for these $U$-statistics, in which each graph contributes to a Wiener chaos of order equal to its number of connected components. We note that the row-column jackknife variance estimator, although nonnegative, does not generally give a studentized statistic with a standard normal limit in degenerate regimes. We illustrate our theory with an application to estimation and testing based on a distance from product form, exhibiting Gaussian and non-Gaussian limits at various rates depending on the model. We also propose a conservative inference procedure that does not require a Gaussian limit, valid under additional moment and projection conditions.

papers.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.

papers.title: AOP-Smart-Finder: A High-Throughput Human-AI Hybrid Framework for AOP Discovery and Evidence Mapping from Large-Scale Literature
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature and the high heterogeneity of biological terminology and mechanistic descriptions make it difficult for researchers to integrate scattered research evidence, identify connections among biological events, and construct mechanistic networks. Here, we developed a high-throughput human-AI hybrid framework, AOP-Smart-Finder, for biological event discovery, relationship mining, and Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) construction and evidence mapping from large-scale literature. This framework integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), AOP-Smart retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technology, and Python-based automation, supporting two analysis modes: one based on a single compound and the other based on a predefined set of biological events. In the di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) case, the system processed 12,983 articles within 30 min and included 1,093 of them, from which it extracted 1,589 biological events (including 458 official key events [KEs] and 1,131 candidate KEs) and 2,519 key event relationships (KERs). In the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) case, the system identified 55 stressors from 437 articles and extracted 278 biological events and 548 event relationships. Following manual curation and Weight of Evidence (WoE) evaluation, a mechanistic network comprising 16 KEs and 23 KERs was ultimately constructed. This framework can either use existing AOPs as knowledge guidance for mechanistic expansion and evidence supplementation, or discover novel event connections and construct mechanistic networks around user-specified research topics. It provides a high-throughput, traceable, human-AI hybrid methodology for complex biological mechanism elucidation and AOP discovery driven by large-scale literature.

papers.title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
papers.abstract: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

papers.title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
papers.abstract: A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them. METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy. SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them. CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.

papers.title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records
papers.abstract: Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.

papers.title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes
papers.abstract: We investigate the upper tail of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$, where $X$ is a centred Gaussian process (GP) with continuous sample paths on a nonempty compact metric space $\mathcal T$. As suggested by the findings of [1], the exponential rate is governed by an optimal-measure problem, while the exact prefactor depends on the local geometry of the corresponding contact set. In the full-contact regime, we strengthen the known Gumbel max-domain of attraction property of the distribution of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$ by establishing the von Mises condition. For fractional Brownian motion on $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, with Hurst index $H\in(0,1/2)$, we also determine the order of the logarithmic correction to the leading Gaussian exponential. For finite contact sets, we distinguish dominated, smooth-critical, and rough-critical regimes and derive exact asymptotics of $P\{\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)>u\}$ as $u\to\infty$ under suitable local assumptions. We illustrate our findings with examples including fractional Brownian motion and the fractional Brownian sheet.

papers.title: Zero Replacement and Latent Profiles in Short Media Diaries: Checking Recording Status Before User Segmentation
papers.abstract: Short media diaries contain many zeros because many activities go unrecorded during the observation period. Log-ratio analysis of time allocation requires these zeros to be replaced with small positive values; as a result, all respondents who did not record an activity receive nearly the same value. We examined how such zero replacement affects classification in latent profile analysis and propose checks to perform before profiles are interpreted. Three-day diaries of 8,089 adults from the 2025 Korea Media Panel Survey were converted into nine-part time-use compositions. Gaming was not recorded by 88.9% of the respondents, and in every model with two to eight profiles and a covariance matrix held equal across profiles, respondents who recorded gaming and those who did not were classified into different profiles. Even when the replacement value equaled the minimum recording unit (5 min/day), the two-profile classification largely matched gaming recording status, and the two groups separated more sharply as the replacement value decreased, until the separation was complete. Before naming profiles, researchers should therefore check the proportion of respondents who did not record each activity and its replacement value, the same proportion within each profile, and the distribution of usage time among those who recorded the activity.

papers.title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability
papers.abstract: In this article, we study heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian-process surrogates, namely Student-$t$ processes, $α$-stable processes and Gaussian processes with heavy-tailed noise. These are Gaussian scale mixtures, and the position of the mixing variable decides whether the tails can be learned from a single realization. For process-level mixtures with a free amplitude, the profile likelihood of the mixing law is data-free and is maximized by the Gaussian law, the plug-in predictive is a data-free transformation of the Gaussian-process predictive, and no estimator can be consistent for the mixing law over the model along one path. For observation-level mixtures with symmetric $α$-stable noise, the tail index is identifiable. Further, for one-dimensional inputs under fixed-domain asymptotics with $α_0<2$ and compact hyperparameter sets, a cross-fitted plug-in estimator and the Laplace marginal-likelihood estimate computed at the global posterior mode attain the efficiency bound of the model with a known regression function, also for Matérn-$5/2$ sample paths. We also characterize small-sample failures of the Laplace approximation as folds of a posterior-mode branch and give a diagnostic. Finally, in a repeated Bayesian optimization study, observation-level tails reduced regret under gross outliers, as did Student-$t$ noise, and no degradation was detected under Gaussian noise.

papers.title: Testing Conditional Moment Restrictions in Networks
papers.abstract: Parametric models of network formation, such as dyadic logit models, are increasingly popular, but few tools exist to test their specification. This paper develops a specification test for conditionally independent dyad (CID) models based on the probabilities that these models assign to subgraphs, the patterns of links among small groups of agents. Given the agents' characteristics, a parametric CID model determines not only the probability of each link but also the probability that a group of agents forms a triangle, a star, or any other subgraph. Under correct specification, the expected frequency of each subgraph among agents with given characteristics equals its model-implied probability. This forms the basis of the testable conditional moment restrictions. The test statistic is the weighted integrated squared distance between a nonparametric kernel estimate of these probabilities and the probabilities implied by the estimated parametric model. I derive its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis.

papers.title: Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations
papers.abstract: A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz '96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.

papers.title: Combining rock typing and NMR logging to estimate permeability in complex carbonate formations
papers.abstract: Estimating intrinsic permeability from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logs is difficult in heterogeneous carbonates because a single calibration may not represent distinct pore systems. We evaluated whether flow-zone-indicator (FZI)-based rock typing improves empirical calibration of the modified Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) model in the Arbuckle Group, Kansas. The analysis used 470 depth-matched core-permeability and NMR measurements from the Wellington and Cutter wells. FZI calculated from measured permeability and NMR-derived porosity was grouped using K-means clustering. Six clusters were identified, but one singleton cluster was excluded, leaving five rock types for SDR calibration. Relative to the global model (without clustering), rock-type-specific calibration reduced testing root mean square log-transformed error (RMSLE) from 1.215 to 0.240-0.427 and increased coefficient of determination (CD) from -0.106 to 0.578-0.924. The fitted porosity exponents ranged from 0.053 to 0.521, indicating that porosity provided limited additional information in some rock types and that the SDR parameters should be treated as empirical calibration quantities. Because measured permeability was used to calculate the FZI before the within-cluster splits, these results represent conditional performance for samples with known FZI membership, not blind permeability prediction. Field implementation will require a permeability-independent method for assigning rock types.

papers.title: Agents Propose, Code Verifies, Humans Decide: Verified Agentic Ingestion of Heterogeneous Scientific Tables into Relational Databases
papers.abstract: Public scientific datasets rarely arrive analysis-ready. They arrive as messy folders of wide matrices, long tables, spreadsheets, and per-cohort files whose keys and encodings differ, and every reanalysis must reconnect them first. A coding agent can automate this, but its mistakes can look plausible, and without an audit trail, a mistake that corrupts data can go uncaught. We present an AI-assisted ingestion pipeline built on one rule: LLM agents propose, deterministic code verifies, and humans decide. Narrow agents see compact, citable evidence about the files, never the data, and return typed proposals. A verifier with 39 check types tests each proposal against that evidence in two loops, one for the schema's structure and one for its meaning, and a human reviewer approves the schema and the load. Code compiles PostgreSQL DDL, reshapes the data, quarantines rows it cannot place, records provenance, and reconciles every staged row against the database. On four public biomedical datasets, one held out from development, 9 of 20 first proposals failed a check and every failure was caught: the loops repaired eight, and a one-line reviewer edit fixed the ninth. All 45.1 million values loaded with zero reconciliation gap. Discovering a dataset's structure took 4-7 LLM calls and preparing its data at most one more, costing under $0.50 per dataset. In a separate test, each of nine planted data errors was quarantined with a reason or recorded in an audit log.

papers.title: Cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time models for competing risks, with application to the Antibody Mediated Prevention trials
papers.abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials randomized participants to VRC01, a broadly neutralizing antibody, or placebo; the primary analysis estimated prevention efficacy against overall HIV-1 acquisition and against acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains. All participants were offered daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and PrEP uptake in a trial may differ substantially from uptake in other settings. It is therefore of interest to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of such acquisition under no or limited PrEP uptake. To address these questions, we extend the structural nested cumulative survival time model (SNCSTM), a causal survival model for time-varying treatments, to a cause-specific version. We show that the cause-specific SNCSTM is closely related to the Fine--Gray subdistribution hazard model, and we study identification under two frameworks. The first, based on sequential ignorability, applies when the time-varying treatment is distinct from the randomized assignment, as with oral PrEP use in AMP. The second, based on an instrumental variable, applies when the time-varying treatment represents compliance with the randomized assignment, and it accommodates unmeasured confounding between the time-varying treatment and event time. Under both frameworks, we propose consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the structural parameters. We apply the methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two AMP trials, to estimate the effects of oral PrEP use and of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains. We also estimate the counterfactual strain-specific cumulative incidence curves under no oral PrEP use and under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.

papers.title: Choosing the basis to compare multivariate distributions: bases, copulas and optimal transport
papers.abstract: We study the choice of an orthonormal basis for comparing two probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ through their one-dimensional projections. We show that two distributions have a common copula in a given basis if and only if their optimal transport can be performed componentwise along the directions of that basis. This motivates the notion of componentwise related distributions and leads to a structural analysis of the bases in which such a representation is possible. In particular, we establish an essential uniqueness result for the corresponding orthogonal decomposition and characterize elliptical families through equality in Gelbrich's bound within location-scatter families. For general distributions, we consider the maximum, over all orthonormal bases, of the sum of the squared quadratic Wasserstein distances between the corresponding one-dimensional projections. We prove that the resulting quantity is a metric, induces the same topology as the quadratic Wasserstein distance, and lies between the Gelbrich and Wasserstein distances, with equality in the upper bound precisely for component-wise related distributions. We also derive first-order conditions for an optimal basis and establish stability and almost-sure consistency of empirical optimal bases. Simulations and examples illustrate the computational feasibility and competitive performance of the proposed procedures and suggest new applications of copulas to multivariate distributional comparisons.
